edge_cases.scenario: A consumer defaulted on a verbal personal loan in 2019 and made no payments for four years; in 2024 a collector persuaded her to make a single $25 'good faith' payment over the phone. The collector sued in 2025 and she wants to know if the suit is time-barred.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node treats 'date of last payment' as the accrual date without qualification, so it would restart the 2-year clock from the 2024 token payment and report the suit as timely. California law is materially more nuanced: under CCP § 360 a new promise must be in a signed writing, and a part payment restarts/revives the period only if made under circumstances showing the debtor acknowledged the whole debt and intended to pay the balance — a payment coaxed by a collector after the period has already run frequently does not revive an already-barred claim. Solicited token payments on stale debt are a standard collection tactic, so this is both common and outcome-determinative; neither the logic nor the checklist distinguishes payments made before expiration from payments made after.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer is served with a collection complaint on a verbal loan that clearly defaulted three years ago. The node tells her the claim is 'expired,' so she ignores the summons, assuming an expired claim cannot result in a judgment. The collector takes a default judgment and begins wage garnishment.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node outputs a bare 'expired' determination with no indication that the California statute of limitations is an affirmative defense that is waived unless raised in a timely answer or demurrer (CCP § 458 / § 430.30). Default judgments are the overwhelmingly typical outcome in California consumer-debt cases, so an 'expired' answer without the accompanying 'you must appear and plead it' instruction is affirmatively misleading and can cost the user the very defense the node identified.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor defaulted on a verbal loan from a family friend in March 2022, filed Chapter 13 in mid-2022, and the case was dismissed without discharge 18 months later. The creditor filed suit in early 2025.
edge_cases.gap_description: The determination compares filing date to accrual + 2 years with no tolling input other than CCP § 351 absence, and the checklist asks no question about bankruptcy. It would report the 2025 filing as time-barred, when the automatic stay period (11 U.S.C. § 362, with the § 108(c) extension and CCP § 356 tolling for a statutory prohibition on suit) very plausibly keeps the claim alive. The tolling_note acknowledges the mechanism exists but neither the logic nor the intake checklist captures the fact needed to apply it, and prior dismissed consumer bankruptcies are common among defendants in these suits.

edge_cases.scenario: A California homeowner with roughly $500,000 of equity files a Chapter 7 bankruptcy petition; she moved to California from Texas and bought the home about two years before filing. She asks how much of her home equity is protected from her creditors.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node encodes only the CCP § 704.730 state-law formula and does not flag the bankruptcy overlay, where the homestead exemption is most often actually litigated. In bankruptcy, 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)'s 730-day domicile rule can force use of another state's (or the federal) exemptions, and § 522(p)'s cap (~$190k–$215k, inflation-adjusted) limits the exemption for a homestead acquired within 1,215 days of filing; § 522(o) can reduce it for equity from fraudulent transfers. Applied as encoded, the rule would tell this debtor she is protected up to the county-median figure (potentially $600k+) when federal law caps her at roughly a third of that — a materially wrong answer.

edge_cases.scenario: A homeowner is facing a forced judicial sale of his residence, but the claim being enforced is a judgment for child and spousal support arrears held by his ex-spouse; a second homeowner in the same posture faces a recorded federal tax lien and threatened IRS foreclosure on the residence.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist omits any dispositive fact about the nature of the claim or lien. Homestead protection is not uniform across claim types: under CCP § 703.070 the exemption as against a support judgment is set by the court under § 703.580 rather than fixed at the statutory figure, and a federal tax lien overrides state homestead exemptions entirely under the Supremacy Clause and 26 U.S.C. § 7403 (as do consensual deeds of trust, purchase-money and mechanics' liens, and HOA assessment liens). The node's 'ordinary money judgment' qualifier is buried in the determination and is not surfaced as a required fact, so a debtor in any of these very common postures would be told a fixed dollar amount of equity is safe when it is not.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor in a county where the exemption computes to $400,000 has a home worth $700,000 with a $300,000 first mortgage — $400,000 of equity, essentially equal to the exemption — and a judgment creditor has levied and set an execution sale. The debtor wants to know whether the house will be sold.
edge_cases.gap_description: The determination's framing ('equity up to the computed amount is protected') implies that a debtor whose equity meets or exceeds the exemption may lose the home, but CCP §§ 704.780 and 704.800 prohibit the sale altogether unless a bid exceeds the sum of liens, costs, and the exemption, and bar re-levy for one year if no qualifying bid appears. The node captures the dollar formula but not the operative outcome rule, so a debtor with equity at or modestly above the exemption is told the wrong practical answer (house sold, excess taken) when in fact the sale is typically blocked entirely.

Steering her to a CCP § 418.10 motion to quash gets it denied and, because the motion tolls nothing after denial in the way she expects, risks default. edge_cases.scenario: A tenant has a default judgment of possession entered against her in justice court in an eviction (forcible detainer) suit after she missed the hearing, and she asks eight days later whether she can get it reopened.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node treats all justice court defaults as governed by TRCP 505.3 (14-day motion to set aside / new trial). Eviction cases are governed by the Rule 510 series, which displaces inconsistent Part V rules: TRCP 510.8(e) bars a motion for new trial in an eviction case entirely, and the remedy is a de novo appeal to county court within 5 days of judgment (TRCP 510.9), with a statement of inability to pay available in lieu of bond. Advising this tenant she has 14 days to file a motion for new trial is affirmatively wrong on both the available remedy and the deadline, and by day 8 the actual 5-day appeal window has already closed (though a late-filed appeal bond/statement issue and possession-bond timing may still matter). Eviction defaults are among the most common default judgments in Texas.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer defaulted in a justice court debt-buyer suit; he learns of the judgment on day 18 after it was signed (he did have notice within 20 days, so TRCP 306a does not help) and asks what he can do.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist treats the justice-court filing deadline as a dispositive gate that forecloses relief once missed, but omits the de novo appeal route: TRCP 506.1 allows appeal from a justice court judgment to county court within 21 days of the judgment (or of denial of a motion for new trial), with a sworn statement of inability to pay in place of a bond, and that appeal vacates the judgment and produces an entirely new trial without any Craddock showing. Telling this person the 14-day window closed the path is materially wrong -- he has a superior, non-discretionary remedy with three days left. This is a deterministic gate of exactly the kind the node otherwise commits to surfacing.

edge_cases.scenario: A defendant was served by citation by publication (a divorce, tax-foreclosure, or quiet-title style case) after the plaintiff filed an affidavit of diligent search; he learns of the default judgment six months later when it shows up on a title search, and service by publication was procedurally proper.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's escape hatches are TRCP 306a (max 90 days from signing) and the Peralta/defective-service path. Neither fits: publication service, if properly executed, is valid service, so Peralta does not apply, and 306a's 90-day outer limit has passed. The node omits TRCP 329, which gives a defendant served only by publication who did not appear a full two years after the judgment is signed to move for a new trial on a sworn showing of good defense. Applying the encoded rule would tell this person the motion-for-new-trial path is dead and steer him to a bill of review, when a much simpler and more favorable statutory remedy is squarely available.

results.derivation_summary: Under the Texas Constitution, current wages for personal service can never be garnished, with only two exceptions: court-ordered child support payments and court-ordered spousal maintenance. The statutory counterpart repeats this rule, providing that current wages are not subject to garnishment except as otherwise provided by state or federal law, and requiring the garnishee (typically the employer) to be discharged from the garnishment as to any current-wage debt owed to the defendant. edge_cases.scenario: A judgment debtor with a $40,000 balance in a savings account, $25,000 in a brokerage account, and $8,000 in cryptocurrency (single adult, no dependents) asks whether a judgment creditor can seize these, reasoning that the total is under the $50,000 cap. The node computes 'aggregate value under the cap' and reports the property as exempt.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node never asks the threshold question of whether the targeted property is even within the § 42.002(a) enumerated list (home furnishings, food, clothing, jewelry, tools of trade, two firearms, sporting equipment, vehicles, livestock/pets, unpaid commissions). Cash, bank deposits, stocks, bonds, crypto, second homes, boats, and collectibles are NOT § 42.002(a) property and are fully non-exempt regardless of the $50,000/$100,000 cap. Checklist item 2 assumes the property is already on the list; nothing prompts the user to verify it. Bank-account and brokerage garnishment is the most common Texas post-judgment collection scenario, so this misstatement of 'under the cap therefore exempt' is squarely wrong for the most typical inquirer.

edge_cases.scenario: A 71-year-old retiree whose only income is Social Security retirement benefits (plus a small VA disability payment) direct-deposited into her checking account is served with a writ of garnishment on that account by a credit-card judgment creditor. She has no IRA and no pension plan.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's only bank-account discussion is the 'current wages lose their character on deposit' note, and its unlimited categories cover § 42.0021 qualified plans but not Social Security, VA, SSI, or other federal benefits. Applied as encoded, it would tell this debtor her deposited benefits are unprotected non-exempt funds. In fact 42 U.S.C. § 407, 38 U.S.C. § 5301, and the anti-garnishment rule at 31 C.F.R. pt. 212 (requiring banks to auto-protect two months of direct-deposited federal benefits) make these funds exempt and largely self-executing. Benefit-recipient debtors are an extremely common garnishment target, and the wrong answer here could cause someone to abandon a valid, dispositive defense.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor who moved from Illinois to Houston 10 months ago files Chapter 7 in the Southern District of Texas and asks whether her $60,000 of household goods, tools, and vehicles is protected as a single mother of two (i.e., under the $100,000 family cap).
edge_cases.gap_description: The node has no bankruptcy-context input at all. Under 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A), a debtor domiciled in Texas for less than 730 days before filing must use the exemptions of the state where she was domiciled for the greater part of the 180 days preceding that period (here Illinois, with far smaller personal-property allowances), or the federal § 522(d) set. The node would confidently apply the $100,000 Texas family cap and produce a materially wrong answer; separately, it never flags that a Texas bankruptcy debtor may elect the federal exemption scheme instead. Interstate movers filing bankruptcy in Texas are common given in-migration volumes.

edge_cases.scenario: A debt buyer sues a consumer for a $27,500 credit-card balance, so the case is filed in county court at law rather than justice court. The defendant, served by a private process server, looks up the Texas answer deadline for a debt-collection suit.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node encodes only the justice-court 14-day rule with no branch for suits above the $20,000 ceiling, where TRCP 99 applies (answer due by 10:00 a.m. on the Monday next following the expiration of 20 days after service). Debt-collection suits above $20,000 are common, and a defendant given '14 days' would either answer needlessly early or, worse, receive a deadline structure that does not match the citation, undermining reliance. The checklist collects the amount but the logic supplies no correct alternative or explicit out-of-scope refusal.

edge_cases.scenario: A justice-court debt claim defendant is served not in person but by certified mail, return receipt requested (or by substituted service under Rule 106(b), e.g., taped to the door plus mailing). She wants to know when her answer is due and from what date she counts.
edge_cases.gap_description: The logic and checklist define the trigger as 'delivery by constable or process server,' with no handling of the alternative service methods expressly authorized in justice court (registered/certified mail under Rule 501.2, substituted service under Rule 106). A mail-served defendant has no 'date of delivery by a constable/process server' to supply, and may count from the mailing date or believe the rule does not apply to her; the encoding gives no rule for identifying the operative service date in these very common scenarios.

edge_cases.scenario: A debt buyer's justice-court petition pleads $18,900 in principal, plus pre-judgment interest and $5,100 in contractual attorney's fees, for a total prayer of about $24,500. The defendant reports the 'amount claimed' as $24,500.
edge_cases.gap_description: The justice-court jurisdictional ceiling is $20,000 exclusive of interest, statutory or punitive damages, penalties, attorney's fees and costs. The encoded checklist asks only for the flat 'amount claimed' and the logic tests it against a $20,000 ceiling, so a case squarely within justice-court jurisdiction will be misclassified as outside it, causing the defendant to be told the 14-day rule does not apply (or to be pointed toward the 20-day county-court timeline) and potentially to blow the real 14-day deadline. Debt claims pleading attorney's fees and interest on top of principal are the norm, not an outlier.
